definition: Conversion rates that adjust for price differences between countries, so an amount buys the same basket of goods and services everywhere. Because many things are cheaper in poorer countries, incomes in PPP terms are usually much higher than at market exchange rates, and they compare living standards better.
The unit of PPP figures: a dollar with the buying power a US dollar had in the United States in the base year (e.g. 2021 PPP). Comparable across countries, not across base years.
Converting a country's figures into dollars at the actual exchange rate. Right for trade and debt; understates living standards in poorer countries, where many goods are cheaper (see PPP).
The World Bank's line for extreme poverty: $3.00 per person per day in 2021 PPP dollars. Older figures used $2.15 (2017 PPP) or $1.90 (2011 PPP); rates on different lines can't be compared.
The share of people living below a poverty line. It says how many are poor, not how poor they are, and is different from the number of poor people.
How far below the poverty line the poor are, on average, as a share of the line — counting everyone else as zero. It measures the depth of poverty, not just how many people are poor.
Like the poverty gap, but large shortfalls count much more than small ones, so it also reflects inequality among the poor.
The Foster-Greer-Thorbecke family of poverty measures: the headcount ratio, the poverty gap, and the squared poverty gap.
Poverty and inequality figures come from household surveys, which many countries run only every few years. A country's latest figure can be several years old, so always check the year.
A summary of income or consumption inequality: 0 means everyone has the same, 100 (or 1) means one person has everything. Most countries fall between about 25 and 60.
The income share of the richest 10% divided by that of the poorest 40%. Higher means more unequal.
A chart of the share of total income held by the poorest x% of people. The further it bows below the diagonal, the more unequal the distribution; the Gini index is based on that gap.
The UN's summary of development from 0 to 1, combining health (life expectancy), education (expected and average years of schooling) and income (GNI per person, PPP).
Gross domestic product: the value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a year.
Gross national income: GDP plus income residents earn abroad, minus income sent to foreigners. Can differ a lot from GDP where foreign-owned firms or remittances are large.
Divided by the population, so countries of different sizes can be compared.
Values adjusted for inflation to the prices of one base year, so changes reflect real quantities. Growth rates should use these, not current prices.
Values in each year's own prices, not adjusted for inflation. Their growth mixes real growth with price increases.
The steady yearly growth rate that would take a value from its starting level to its ending level over the period.
How many years something takes to double at a given growth rate — roughly 70 divided by the growth rate in percent (the rule of 70).
The difference between two percentages: from 10% to 12% is a rise of 2 percentage points, which is a 20% increase.

The part of output growth not explained by more capital or more (and better-educated) workers — often read as technology and efficiency. It is measured as a residual, so it also absorbs measurement errors.
Splitting growth in output per worker into contributions from more capital per worker, more schooling (human capital), and TFP.
Workers' skills and knowledge. In the Penn World Table it is an index based on years of schooling and the estimated returns to education.
Poorer countries growing faster than richer ones and catching up (beta convergence), or the spread of incomes across countries shrinking (sigma convergence).
The shift of workers and output from agriculture into industry and services as economies develop.
Children under 5 whose height for their age is more than two standard deviations below the WHO growth standard — a sign of long-term undernutrition.
The probability that a newborn dies before age 5, per 1,000 live births.
The average number of years a newborn would live if death rates at each age stayed as they are now.
The average number of children a woman would have over her lifetime if current birth rates at each age continued.
The World Bank's four country groups by GNI per person (Atlas method, at market exchange rates), updated every July.
The share of working-age people who have a job. It is not 100 minus the unemployment rate: people not looking for work count as neither employed nor unemployed.
The share of working-age people who are working or looking for work.
The percentage rise in prices over a year, usually measured by the consumer price index (CPI).
A projection, not a measurement. Growth forecasts here come from the World Bank's Global Economic Prospects, and each edition revises the last.
Money that migrants send to their families in their home country.
A study that randomly decides who gets a program, so differences between the groups can be attributed to the program itself.
Money given directly to households. Conditional transfers require something in return (e.g. children attending school); unconditional ones don't.
Small loans (and other financial services) for poor households and small businesses that banks usually don't serve.
Large household surveys run in about 90 developing countries every ~5 years, on health, nutrition, fertility, and education.
The average income rank reached as adults by children who grew up in low-income families (parents at the 25th percentile). Higher means poor children do better there.
How much children's incomes or positions differ from their parents'. High mobility means where you start matters less.
How closely two measures move together, from -1 to 1. It shows association, not cause: both may be driven by something else.
